source.title: Cascaded Sparse Autoencoders Learn Multi-Level Visual Concepts in Multimodal LLMs
source.authors: Yu-Song Zhao; Heng-Yi Wang; Tanuja Ganu; A. Nambi; Hao Wang

record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature analysis to visual representations in multimodal LLMs and reports semantic-coherence results on those models, a new setting beyond toy networks.
record.gate_note: The paper trains SAEs on MLLM visual activations and evaluates hierarchical semantic coherence (HMS); the reported HMS measurements are included. It also reports intentional concept-steering outcomes, recorded separately as findings not covered by the claim versions. Cited findings from other studies are not included. Numerous other SAE baselines and HMSmed results are omitted under the 60-row limit.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It uses SAEs as a tool to propose SAE++, a cascaded hierarchical SAE, and reports only its own method's hierarchical-coherence (HMS) and steering performance against other SAE variants. HMS measures whether Level-1 SAE features grouped under one Level-2 parent have similar image-embedding semantics. It does not measure whether features are superposed or spread across neurons, or whether the model contains sparse features an SAE recovers better than a neuron basis. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAE++ (a Level-2 SAE trained on Level-1 decoder atoms) yields more coherent hierarchical visual concepts than flat, Matryoshka and stacked SAE baselines across three MLLMs and four datasets, and enables effective group-level steering. They also give theoretical arguments for failure modes of stacked and Matryoshka designs, and note limits including dependence on Level-1 SAE quality and that HMS does not penalize duplicate concepts.
record.recipe_differences: This is an SAE-based study of hierarchical visual concepts in MLLMs, not a reproduction of the toy-network setup or measurements in Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported HMS varies by model and dataset. The paper does not report systematic sensitivity sweeps over SAE architectures, sparsity levels, expansion ratios, layers, or training datasets; it identifies these as future analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Level-1 SAE decoder directions in MLLM visual activations can be grouped by a second SAE into semantically coherent higher-level clusters. SAE++ HMSmean is 0.74–0.99 across 12 settings versus lower scores for flat, Matryoshka and stacked SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature directions in MLLMs have a learnable hierarchical (parent–child) semantic organization.

fits_no_version.finding: Deliberately clamping a group of SAE++ features shifts target-concept presence in Qwen3-VL captions: insertion averages 71.0% vs 11.1% without steering, suppression 40.1% vs 0.0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Group-level SAE feature steering controls concept presence in MLLM outputs.

record.problems: HMS measures semantic similarity using embeddings from a fixed vision backbone and does not exhaust other notions of hierarchy or explicitly penalize duplicate concepts. The study covers three model families and four visual datasets; HMS tables report no uncertainty estimates. Steering evaluates a limited set of concepts and relies on LLM judges. The authors say performance depends on Level-1 SAE quality and that sensitivity to several design choices is not systematically studied.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted HMSmed results and results for other individual SAE baselines to stay within the row limit; these are in Section 5.2 and Appendix F, Tables 14–16. Omitted steering comparator rows (no-steering, random, Matryoshka, and single-feature methods) from Table 3; their values are not needed to report the SAE++ steering result. Additional steering variability and off-target checks are in Appendix D, Tables 7–9.

untested.parts: No toy-model experiment, sparsity transition or geometry analysis.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Does not measure feature spread across neurons. Does not compare SAE recovery with a neuron basis. Assumes rather than tests that SAEs recover sparse features.
No completeness, stability or canonicity test of SAE features (the only training-stability check is loss curves from one run).
Treats decoder columns as 1-D directions without testing this against multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper's results are performance comparisons of its own SAE architecture; all HMS rows are own-method or baseline-method scores and should not be linked to V4. The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed. Superposition is invoked only as motivation (citing Toy Models of Superposition).

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network superposition experiment or test of a sparsity-dependent transition or regular superposition geometry.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons result from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

Tests visual SAE features in MLLMs using hierarchical semantic-coherence metrics; it does not measure whether features are distributed across neurons, compare against a one-feature-per-neuron account, or establish the completeness of SAE recovery.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable across runs or settings, or canonical units.
Uses decoder columns as feature directions but does not test one-dimensional against multidimensional feature representations.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE++ visual hierarchies across Qwen3-VL, Gemma-3, and LLaVA on Color, ImageNet, COCO, and iNaturalist
reader_labels.reason: HMSmean is reported as high for SAE++ in all 12 model–dataset settings, indicating semantically coherent groupings of SAE-derived visual concepts; see H-Q-C-PP through H-L-N-PP. This supports semantic feature recovery in the tested visual setting, not a general claim about feature distribution or completeness.
